chapter: Teschemacher, Pee Wee, Noon and Simeon
title: Omer Simeon as an influence on white Chicago clarinetists
summary: Chace feels Simeon's ease and ensemble playing foreshadow the hot Chicago style, and doubts that Jelly Roll wrote out the Red Hot Peppers parts.

bands.name: Jelly Roll Morton's Red Hot Peppers

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: You see a closer relationship, do you, between Simeon and the white style than between any of the other...

Somehow I do, and I don't know why, really. But he attacked, he seemed to attack the instrument in a different way than Noon, or Begard, or Darnell Howard, with... How can you put it? What adjectives can you use? He had ease. He knew what he was doing. He was... He didn't... He doesn't ever sound on the jelly roll, red hot pepper, sidesy. He does... He never sounds ill at ease, or nervous, and those are words I think you can use in connection with the Chicago style. But he tended that way. It's very hard to say.
He wasn't usually the soloist on early records, was he? The peppers you talk about might have been the first time that he appeared as a soloist.

For all I know. His ensemble work is excellent. Of course, there's another manner of approach to the style, the method of playing ensemble. Now, they tell me that Jelly wrote out all the parts of the red hot peppers. I don't believe it. It's impossible. But Simeon would move around in the ensembles in a way that kind of forecasts the hot style of playing.
